Footer.note: Testnet prototype. Real STs and stablecoins can only be issued by licensed entities.

HomePage.title: Same 100%, different outcome
HomePage.lead: Occupancy is 100% on both. The numbers are identical. Yet one can be pledged as collateral and the other is refused by the contract.
HomePage.why: A prospectus always attaches a basis and an as-of date to a figure — "gross floor area (land registry)", "occupancy (by area)". On the operator's site those qualifiers are dropped, leaving a bare number. That difference is what this prototype puts on-chain.
HomePage.surveyLead: 71 real-estate ST filings from EDINET were measured to see who sets the description. Not the trustee bank — the asset manager.

Confidential.title: Deciding without disclosing
Confidential.lead: Prospectuses mark some figures "rent and common charges — not disclosed", because the tenant did not consent. Yet collateral assessment needs the rent. On a confidential EVM the rent can sit on-chain while only the verdict comes back.
Confidential.run: Check whether the rent covers it
Confidential.note: The rent itself is never returned. On an ordinary EVM, reading storage directly reveals it even when the variable is private. On Sapphire it does not. Same code — only the place it runs differs.

Disclaimer.title: About this data
Disclaimer.body: Property names are fictional. Floor area, appraisal value and occupancy follow the public prospectus of three Kenedix logistics properties (May 2025). Rent is a placeholder, since the prospectus marks it as not disclosed. The borrowing power assumes a 50% LTV, which no document supports. This is a testnet prototype, not a real financial product.

Survey.title: Who decides the description
Survey.lead: This prototype assumes that qualifiers get dropped on operator sites. Here is that assumption checked against the actual filings.
Survey.populationLead: 1,323 weekdays of EDINET were queried, yielding 150 registration statements filed as domestic trust beneficiary certificates or investment-business rights.
Survey.populationNote: Document type alone does not separate them: 72 of the same category were equity-index-linked trust bonds. Reclassification used the body text. The same label meaning different things is exactly the problem under study — and this survey walked into it.
Survey.whoLead: The filer is the trustee bank. Does the trustee set the description? Overlap of field names between filings (Jaccard) was measured two ways.
Survey.verdictBody: Grouping by trustee yields +0.04 — no separation. Grouping by asset manager yields +0.36. The trustee supplies the vehicle; the manager writes the description. That changes who a standardisation effort should approach.
Survey.amNote: Kenedix shares 36 fields across its filings — the most consistent. Tosei sits at 0.18 with 3 shared fields, inconsistent even within one manager. A standard is faster to write by copying the most disciplined existing practice than by designing from scratch.
Survey.fieldsLead: How many of the 68 filings each appears in. Green over 90%, amber under 60%.
Survey.universalTitle: Only two fields appear in all 68
Survey.universalBody: Neither area, nor occupancy, nor appraisal value appears everywhere. What all 68 shared:
Survey.l3: Asset manager names are inferred from body text, not verified by eye.
Survey.l4: This covers statutory disclosure only. The operator-site comparison rests on 11 issues checked by hand.
Survey.dataLead: The data behind this survey, released in full — not just the aggregates but the per-filing record of which field names each used.
Survey.dJson: Per-filing records for 68 filings: extracted field names, filer, asset manager, and the collection and extraction method.
Survey.dCsv: Occurrence matrix. Rows are filings, columns are field names (552). 1 means present. Opens directly in a spreadsheet.
Survey.dataNote: CC0. Originals are retrievable from EDINET by docID (no API key needed). Extraction recall is 85–88%, so the matrix contains misses.
Survey.layerLead: For the same properties, what statutory disclosure (layer 1) and operator sites (layer 2) each show, compared mechanically. Layer 2 covers 37 pages swept across six operators.
Survey.qualLead: Fields carrying an explicit basis or as-of date
Survey.qualNote: Counts of qualified labels such as "gross floor area (land registry)" or "occupancy (by area)". Per filing: 2.47 → 0.04. The numbers survive; what they rest on and when they were measured does not.
Survey.layerNote: Five operators have both layers. Retention runs 0–27%. Kenedix is the most detailed in layer 1 (66.6 fields) yet publishes no property table at all — across all 16 issues only "appraisal value" appears. Resona has no layer-1 filing in the set, so no retention figure.
Survey.dL2: Per-page records from operator sites (layer 2): the pages swept across three managers and the fields each showed.
Survey.verifiedLead: The main claim — that asset managers set the description — rested on names inferred from body text. All 68 filings were checked by matching the inferred name against nearby terms such as "asset manager" or "investment management company".
Survey.verifiedResult: 66 matched. Two were wrong and have been corrected. The conclusion is unchanged (+0.36 → +0.37).
Survey.robustLead: Two likely reviewer objections, checked in advance: that field matching is by string, and that extraction misses fields.
Survey.normTitle: Normalization does not change the conclusion — but it has a side effect
Survey.normBody: Stripping the parenthetical qualifiers and folding variants raises the universally-present fields from 2 to 11 (label types 552→438). But that is achieved precisely by discarding the qualifiers this survey argues matter — treating "gross floor area (land registry)" and "(inspection certificate)" as the same thing. Normalization restates the problem rather than solving it.
Survey.valBody: Ground truth was hand-read from the property tables and matched exactly: 174/191 fields, with 4 of 7 at 100%. Misses cluster in two shapes — fields nested under a sub-heading, and labels whose parenthetical spans a line break. Not random.

Vocab.title: A vocabulary for the description
Vocab.lead: Field definitions to make real-estate ST property descriptions machine-readable, derived from 68 filings.
Vocab.howBody: The first plan was to copy the most disciplined practice (Kenedix, 36 shared fields). Measurement killed that: those 36 barely overlap other managers — 7 fields with Mitsui, 3 with Tosei. Kenedix is heavy on appraisal internals and lacks the separate address and lot-number fields others carry. So the base became what seven managers already share, with the qualifier discipline borrowed from wherever it is strongest.
Vocab.p1: A measure is value, basis and as-of date together. Missing any one, it cannot be recorded.
Vocab.p2: Use-specific fields are allowed, but must declare their superordinate concept.
Vocab.p3: Existing wording is not replaced. Original labels stay; they map onto this vocabulary.
Vocab.extensionRule: 1–2 managers. Optional, but define it if published
Vocab.outLead: Things that should not go on-chain, or should go differently.
Vocab.statusBody: Version 0.1, from 68 filings by 7 managers. Extraction recall is 85–88%, so fields are missed. Manager names are inferred from body text. No practitioner has reviewed it.

OnChain.title: What runs on the chain
OnChain.lead: Why this prototype uses a chain at all, in a form you can try. Reading needs no wallet.
OnChain.whyTitle: One difference from an ordinary web app
OnChain.whyBody: Anyone can write without permission, and a write that breaks the declared vocabulary is still refused. Separating who may write from what may be written is the reason to use a chain. Recording is open here — yet "occupancy with land-registry basis" is rejected no matter who sends it.
OnChain.readLead: Everything below is queried from the viewer's browser against a public RPC. The server only ships static files.
OnChain.vLead: The standard itself is on-chain data. Adding a field needs no redeploy. This is not the JSON rendered — it is what is actually deployed.
OnChain.pLead: Who recorded what, when — assembled from chain events. No index server. The record carries its own history.
OnChain.writeLead: Actually write to the chain. Both accepted and rejected combinations are offered, so you can trigger the refusal yourself.
OnChain.tLead: Connect MetaMask or similar. A little Sapphire Testnet gas is needed (free from faucet.testnet.oasis.dev).
OnChain.noWallet: No wallet found. Install MetaMask or similar.
OnChain.tNote: A rejected write costs no gas: estimation fails first, so the transaction is never submitted. Bad data does not merely get flagged — the transaction does not happen.
OnChain.limitBody: Testnet prototype. Anything written here is public and permanent. Do not enter real property data or anything about a person. The property id is fixed to SANDBOX.
OnChain.limit: Sapphire caps log queries at 100 blocks. A confidential chain cannot be scanned freely — the more you hide, the less can be checked afterwards. A write you just made above will appear here.
OnChain.dvpLead: Delivery of the ST and payment settle in a single transaction. You act as the buyer; the seller pre-approved at deployment.
OnChain.dLead: Four steps, because that is the real sequence. Only the last one is DvP — the part a bank transfer cannot do.
OnChain.hRegister: The ST is transfer-restricted; unregistered addresses cannot receive it
OnChain.hMint: Mints the mock coin to yourself (the real one needs a licence)
OnChain.hApprove: Lets the DvP contract pull your yen
OnChain.hSettle: 1 ST and ¥1,000,000 settle in one transaction
OnChain.settleDone: Atomic settlement done. Both legs moved in the same transaction:
OnChain.dNote: Steps 1–3 are ordinary preparation and work the same anywhere. Step 4 is the difference: delivery and payment sit in one transaction, so one cannot happen without the other. A bank transfer always has a moment where the money has left but not arrived. Here that moment does not exist.
OnChain.verBody: Bump the version when the rules change — but records already made are not invalidated retroactively. A value validated under v1 stays a v1 value. Descriptions are made under the rules of their time; overturning past descriptions with new rules destroys the ability to know what was ever correct.
OnChain.signLead: Separate the sender from the attester. For provenance, who said it matters more than who sent it.
OnChain.gLead: Sign the value, then send it. The sender pays gas, but the record keeps the signer.
OnChain.gOther: Recorded as someone else. Altering the value changes the recovered signer:
OnChain.gNote: "Alter the value and send" keeps the signature but shifts the value by one. The signature is bound to the value, so a different signer is recovered — showing the value and its attester stay tied together.
OnChain.hBorrow: Only works where the occupancy basis is declared
